target.title: fix(google): reject malformed provider media base64
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Google provider responses could include malformed inline audio or video base64 that Node would decode permissively instead of rejecting.

## Why This Change Was Made

Google music, speech, and video generation now share a strict base64 decoder before materializing provider-returned media. The Google-specific decoder accepts both standard base64 and Google ProtoJSON-valid base64url payloads before canonical validation, while inline video bytes reuse the existing generated-video byte cap before decode so oversized payloads fail before allocating the full buffer.

## User Impact

Users get a clear provider error for malformed Google media responses without rejecting valid base64url media that Google may return, and operators keep the existing video media cap behavior without permissive base64 decoding.

## Evidence

Live Google TTS run through the production `buildGoogleSpeechProvider().synthesize()` entrypoint; this was captured on the earlier PR head `f36b9f96544a6416e51712ee3881e682409df825` before the base64url compatibility follow-up, and the same entrypoint remains covered by focused regression tests on current head `83a97f97bd373248e4646cc703222d6846494cfa`:

```text
$ GEMINI_API_KEY=<redacted> node node_modules/vitest/vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.extension-providers.config.ts extensions/google/live-google-tts-proof.test.ts --reporter verbose

=== LIVE GOOGLE TTS PROOF ===
entrypoint=buildGoogleSpeechProvider().synthesize
started_at=2026-07-14T12:47:34.918Z
model=gemini-3.1-flash-tts-preview
voice=Kore
proxy=explicit-redacted
api_key=redacted
ok=true
output_format=wav
file_extension=.wav
audio_bytes=109484
pcm_payload_bytes=109440
wav_header=RIFF/WAVE
```

The focused tests drive the real exported provider entrypoints — `buildGoogleSpeechProvider().synthesize()`, `buildGoogleMusicGenerationProvider().generateMusic()`, and `buildGoogleVideoGenerationProvider().generateVideo()` — with crafted valid, malformed, and oversized provider responses; the `decodeGoogleProviderBase64` guard runs as real production code on that response path:

- **Valid path preserved:** legitimate standard base64 and base64url audio/video still materialize; the video byte cap reuses the existing generated-video limit rather than a new arbitrary value, so valid traffic is not truncated.
- **Malformed rejected:** music, speech, and video malformed inline base64 each raise a provider-specific error instead of decoding corrupt bytes.
- **Oversized rejected before buffering:** inline video bytes, direct URI downloads, and SDK file-handle downloads exceeding the media cap fail before unbounded allocation.


target.title: fix: block unresolved Telegram reply targets
target.body:
## Summary

Adds a Telegram reply-target preflight so OpenClaw does not start an agent turn when Telegram reports a reply target but the assembled context did not recover usable replied-to content.

The guard treats `[unsupported Telegram rich_message received]` as unresolved context rather than as a usable reply body. In that case, the runner returns a clarification instead of letting the model infer intent from nearby conversation history.

## What Problem This Solves

A user can reply to an older bot/flow message, but if the replied-to message is represented only as an unsupported rich-message placeholder, the agent may answer using nearby context from a different message. This is especially risky for short replies like “what changed?”, “do it”, “1”, or “3”.

Expected behavior: if `ReplyToId` exists for a Telegram turn, OpenClaw should either provide usable replied-to context to the agent or block and ask for the missing context. It should not guess from nearby messages.

## Behavior

- Blocks Telegram turns with `ReplyToId` when the only reply body is `[unsupported Telegram rich_message received]`.
- Allows Telegram turns when `ReplyToBody` has usable text.
- Allows Telegram turns when a selected chat-window structured context includes the reply target with usable text.
- Does not affect non-Telegram channels.

## Evidence

Focused regression coverage was added in `src/auto-reply/reply/get-reply-run.reply-target-preflight.test.ts` for the unresolved Telegram rich-message placeholder shape and the allowed cases where reply context is usable.

Local verification:

```text

```

## Related

target.title: fix(cron): bound cron quarantine sidecar file reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`loadCronQuarantineFile` in `src/cron/store.ts` reads the cron quarantine sidecar with an unbounded `fs.promises.readFile` call. A corrupted or hostile quarantine file could force the cron load path to buffer an arbitrarily large file into memory, leading to OOM.

## Why This Change Was Made

Quarantine sidecars are small JSON files. An 8 MiB cap is generous headroom for legitimate quarantine state while preventing the cron load path from being used as a memory exhaustion vector.

## User Impact

Loading a cron quarantine file that exceeds the safe cap now fails fast with a clear size-limit error instead of risking process OOM.

## Evidence

- Added a regression test that writes a quarantine file exceeding the 8 MiB cap and asserts `loadCronQuarantineFile` rejects with `File exceeds 8388608 bytes`.
- Local focused run: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/cron/store.test.ts --run` passes (47/47 tests).


## Real behavior proof

I ran a standalone non-test script that imports the real `loadCronQuarantineFile` from `src/cron/store.ts`, creates a valid sidecar, then creates an 8 MiB + 1 byte sidecar and attempts to load both.

Command:

```text
$ node --import tsx /tmp/proof-101477.mjs
```

Output:

```text
=== Normal quarantine sidecar ===
path: /tmp/proof-cron-quarantine-normal-1783420207397.json
loaded: {
  "version": 1,
  "jobs": [
    {
      "quarantinedAtMs": 1783420207397,
      "sourceIndex": 0,
      "reason": "invalid schedule",
      "job": {
        "id": "test-job",
        "schedule": "not-a-cron"
      }
    }
  ]
}

=== Oversized quarantine sidecar ===
path: /tmp/proof-cron-quarantine-oversized-1783420207397.json
size: 8388609 bytes (> 8388608 byte cap)
rejected: File exceeds 8388608 bytes: /tmp/proof-cron-quarantine-oversized-1783420207397.json
```

The normal sidecar loads and parses successfully. The oversized sidecar is rejected before any JSON parsing or downstream cron processing occurs, with the bounded reader returning `File exceeds 8388608 bytes`.

- Also added a regression test that asserts `saveCronQuarantineFile` rejects before writing a sidecar whose JSON payload would exceed the same 8 MiB cap, preventing OpenClaw from creating a sidecar it cannot later load.

target.title: fix(cli): bound --message-file reads for agent command
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`readAgentMessageFile` in `src/commands/agent-via-gateway.ts` used `fs.readFile(messageFile)` with no size limit. A user (or a symlink attack) pointing `--message-file` at a multi-gigabyte file could exhaust CLI memory before the message is validated or dispatched.

## Why This Change Was Made

Agent messages are prompt text; a 4 MiB cap is generous headroom for long system prompts while preventing an unbounded local-file read from OOMing the gateway/embedded dispatch path. The existing error formatting is preserved so callers still see familiar ENOENT/EISDIR messages.

## User Impact

- `openclaw agent --message-file <path>` now rejects files larger than 4 MiB with a clear size-limit error.
- Normal message files continue to work unchanged, including UTF-8 BOM stripping.
- The gateway is never reached with an oversized message file.

## Evidence

- Replaced `readFile` with `readRegularFile({ filePath: messageFile, maxBytes: AGENT_MESSAGE_FILE_MAX_BYTES })` in `src/commands/agent-via-gateway.ts`.
- Added a regression test in `src/commands/agent-via-gateway.test.ts` asserting that a 5 MiB message file is rejected before `callGateway` is invoked.
- Lint and core typecheck pass locally. Full test suite will run on the PR CI.

## Real behavior proof

I created a 5 MiB message file and a directory path and ran `agentCliCommand` with `--message-file`. The CLI rejects both before any gateway dispatch:

```text
$ OPENCLAW_VITEST_MAX_WORKERS=1 node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/commands/agent-via-gateway.test.ts --run
[test] starting test/vitest/vitest.commands.config.ts

     ✓ rejects message files that exceed the size cap
     ✓ reports a directory message file with the legacy EISDIR message
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  70 passed (70)
[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 17.16s
```

- The oversized file is rejected with `File exceeds 4194304 bytes` and `callGateway` is never invoked.
- A directory path still reports `Message file is a directory:` preserving the existing CLI UX.

## Real behavior proof (standalone)

Ran a standalone Node script outside Vitest that imports the real `readRegularFile` helper re-exported by `src/infra/regular-file.ts` (the same helper now used by `readAgentMessageFile`) and exercises normal, oversized, and directory inputs:

```text

Temp root: /tmp/proof-101442-24382397-303b-4df6-9e58-5fb8b44c202a

  Normal file read ... OK: decoded="Hello from PR #101442.\n"
  Oversized file rejects ... OK: File exceeds 4194304 bytes: /tmp/proof-101442/huge.md
  Directory rejects as non-regular ... OK: path must be a regular file
  Directory preserves legacy EISDIR UX ... OK: Message file is a directory: /tmp/proof-101442/not-a-file

All real-behavior checks passed.
```

Command used:

```text
node --import ./node_modules/tsx/dist/loader.mjs /tmp/proof-101442.mjs
```

The script is intentionally not committed to the repo and lives at `/tmp/proof-101442.mjs`.



## Real behavior proof (standalone CLI)

I ran the real `openclaw agent --message-file` CLI path (via `pnpm openclaw`) against four temp inputs:

**1. Normal message file**
```text
$ pnpm openclaw agent --local --message-file /tmp/proof-101442-cli/normal.md --session-key agent:test:proof --json
[agent] run 40130106-91a0-47f3-ba23-fa79a807f5c0 ended with stopReason=aborted
```
The CLI read the file and started the agent turn (aborted because no model provider was configured).

**2. Oversized message file (5 MiB, cap is 4 MiB)**
```text
$ pnpm openclaw agent --local --message-file /tmp/proof-101442-cli/huge.md --session-key agent:test:proof --json
Error: Unable to read message file /tmp/proof-101442-cli/huge.md: File exceeds 4194304 bytes: /tmp/proof-101442-cli/huge.md | File exceeds 4194304 bytes: /tmp/proof-101442-cli/huge.md
[ELIFECYCLE] Command failed with exit code 1.
```
The CLI rejected the file before any gateway dispatch or model call.

**3. Single-symlink message file**
```text
$ pnpm openclaw agent --local --message-file /tmp/proof-101442-cli/symlink.md --session-key agent:test:proof --json
[agent] run 9bf5fd4e-8aae-4561-bb6a-4a1ad01be49e ended with stopReason=stop
```

**4. Chained-symlink message file**
```text
$ pnpm openclaw agent --local --message-file /tmp/proof-101442-cli/link-b.md --session-key agent:test:proof --json

```
The full symlink chain was resolved and the agent turn started.

The implementation now uses `fs.realpath` before the bounded read, so legacy symlinked `--message-file` paths continue to work while oversized files are rejected before dispatch.

target.title: fix(doctor): exit non-zero on final invalid config (#77804)
target.body:
## Summary

`openclaw doctor` printed `Invalid config:` validation errors but still exited `0`. CI/CD pipelines and wrapper scripts that key off doctor's exit code to detect an unhealthy configuration were therefore falsely reassured. This PR sets `process.exitCode = 1` from `runFinalConfigValidationHealth` when the final on-disk config snapshot is still invalid, and makes the `doctor` command wrapper at `src/cli/program/register.maintenance.ts` honor `process.exitCode` instead of unconditionally exiting `0`.

Fixes #77804.

The change is small and localized:

- `src/flows/doctor-health-contributions.ts` (+3): set `process.exitCode = 1` only if not already non-zero.
- `src/cli/program/register.maintenance.ts` (+1/-1): pass `process.exitCode` through to `defaultRuntime.exit(...)`.
- `src/flows/doctor-health-contributions.test.ts` (+84): four new vitest cases grafted into main's existing `doctor:final-config-validation` block.
- `src/cli/program/register.maintenance.test.ts` (+19): regression for the command-wrapper exit-code passthrough.

Rebased onto current `main` (was ~12k commits behind). Resolved the test-file conflict by taking main's evolved version and re-grafting the four exit-code cases; dropped the contributor `CHANGELOG.md` entry per repo policy.

## Still-needed validation (against current main)

Confirmed still unfixed upstream: `runFinalConfigValidationHealth` on current `main` reads the final snapshot and prints `Invalid config:` issues but never sets `process.exitCode`, and the `doctor` wrapper still calls `defaultRuntime.exit(0)` unconditionally.

## Real behavior proof

target.title: docs: respect configured Crabbox provider for agent tests
target.body:
Related: #104485

## What Problem This Solves

Ordinary Crabbox agent commands were forced onto Blacksmith Testbox even when an operator had selected another eligible provider through `CRABBOX_PROVIDER`. That made machine-local provider preferences ineffective and could also cause local-container execution to be described as remote/Testbox proof.

## Why This Change Was Made

Aligns the root policy and both Crabbox/testing skills on one provider-selection contract:

1. Source trust, platform, and proof requirements determine eligible providers.
2. An explicit eligible provider requested by the user wins.
3. Ordinary eligible wrapper calls omit `--provider`, allowing `CRABBOX_PROVIDER` to override the repository default.
4. With no user or environment preference, Blacksmith Testbox remains the repository fallback.

The same contract is applied to the root policy plus the Crabbox, testing, and PR-maintainer skills, so PR workflows cannot reintroduce mandatory Testbox routing. This restores the original goal of #104485 without weakening the sanitized-AWS/secretless-CI requirements for untrusted source. It is the maintained replacement because the original PR branch could not be updated. Original contributor: @hxy91819.

## User Impact

Operators can set a machine-local preference such as `CRABBOX_PROVIDER=local-container` without changing the shared skill. AWS or another eligible provider can be selected the same way. Task-specific user requests still take priority, while unsafe or platform-incompatible choices remain blocked.

## Evidence

- Current head: `32452922d779597437621cdf63fb02d740b49837`.
- Dependency contract checked in Crabbox source: config files load before environment overrides, `CRABBOX_PROVIDER` overrides the configured provider, and an explicit CLI `--provider` remains the final override.

target.title: fix(acp): keep completed run-mode sessions resumable
target.body:
Closes #106696.

## What Problem This Solves

ACP sessions spawned with `mode="run"` are intentionally closed after their first turn. A later `sessions_send` to the same completed child therefore started a fresh agent conversation or failed with missing ACP metadata instead of resuming the backend conversation. This made parent agents unable to answer questions or continue work in an existing one-shot Codex or Claude session.

## Why This Change Was Made

The manager now retains completed one-shot metadata only when the agent advertises ACP session resume/load support and a stable ACP session ID has been recorded. A parent follow-up resumes that ID, fails closed if resume fails, and keeps OpenClaw's one-shot lifecycle while reconnecting through ACPX under a fresh process lease.

The change also distinguishes a live prompt from terminal cleanup, so a parent can send the supported follow-up as soon as terminal delivery begins. Agents without resume support and one-shots that are still actively prompting remain rejected.

## User Impact

Parents can follow up with completed ACP run-mode children without losing task context. Codex and Claude one-shots preserve their working directory and conversation state across the follow-up, while active turns, unsupported agents, invalid resume targets, and abandoned process ownership remain handled conservatively.

## Evidence

Validated on Node 24.18.0 after rebasing onto current `main`:

- changed ACPX runtime test: 59 tests passed
- ACP configuration lane: 66 tests passed
- targeted ACP manager, task-registry, session-meta, and sessions-tool shards passed
- `pnpm tsgo:core`, changed-file `oxfmt`, changed-file `oxlint`, and `git diff --check` passed
- `codex review --base upstream/main` was run locally and its findings were addressed
- The full `pnpm test:extension acpx` lane reported 172 passing tests and four unrelated failures already present on current `main`: the new Pi session-catalog API is missing from three plugin test fixtures, and its manifest schema snapshot has not yet been updated. This PR does not modify those surfaces.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** A completed ACP `mode="run"` child lost its original conversation when the parent later used `sessions_send`, causing a fresh-session response or `ACP_SESSION_INIT_FAILED` instead of a contextual follow-up.
- **Real environment tested:** A Linux system running a long-lived OpenClaw gateway from a local build with the bundled ACPX extension, using both Claude ACP and Codex ACP child sessions launched by a parent agent.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:** Spawned a one-shot child that returned a unique context marker, waited for the run to complete and its runtime process to be cleaned up, then sent a follow-up through `sessions_send` to the same OpenClaw ACP session key asking for the marker. Repeated the flow for Claude and Codex.
- **Evidence after fix:** The initial child output contained `CONTEXT_TOKEN=<redacted-marker>`. The later follow-up returned the same marker under the same OpenClaw ACP session key and backend transcript ID. Neither follow-up reported a fresh session or missing task context.
- **Observed result after fix:** Completed Claude and Codex one-shots resumed their original backend conversation and answered the parent follow-up with the prior context intact. An actually active one-shot was still rejected, and an invalid resume target failed closed rather than silently starting fresh.
- **What was not tested:** Windows and macOS were not exercised in the real setup. The final stale-`closed` process-lease recovery and terminal-delivery race refinements were validated with unit/integration tests, not by deliberately crashing the production gateway during those exact windows.

## AI-assisted disclosure

This PR is AI-assisted. I ran the real behavior validation and automated tests, reviewed the implementation and review findings, and understand the metadata, resume-capability, lifecycle, and process-lease changes in this patch.

## Summary

**Problem**: `findSchema.limit` accepts floating-point values via `Type.Number()`, but "Max results" is inherently an integer-valued field. Float values like `limit=5.5` silently pass `Type.Number` validation and reach tool execution with ambiguous behavior.

**Solution**: Tighten `limit` to `Type.Integer()` with a runtime `Number.isSafeInteger` execution guard. **Per ClawSweeper review, `minimum: 1` has been removed** — zero and negative values retain the existing runtime normalization behavior, so the change only rejects fractional (non-integer) values.

**What changed / NOT changed**:
1. Schema: `Type.Number()` → `Type.Integer()` (no minimum constraint)
2. Runtime: `Number.isSafeInteger(limit)` guard rejects non-integer at execution boundary
3. Focused regression tests (10 cases): valid int, float rejection, zero/negative acceptance (preserved normalization), optional, required pattern, execution boundary
4. Root proof script removed per ClawSweeper review

The runtime `Number.isSafeInteger` guard rejects fractional values at the tool-call boundary. `normalizePositiveLimit` handles value clamping. Zero and negative values continue to be normalized at runtime (existing behavior preserved).

target.title: fix(cron): skip deleteAfterRun and preserve counters for manual runs (#83538)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw cron run` (a manual/operator run) on a `deleteAfterRun` one-shot ("at") job used to delete the job on success — consuming the one-shot so its scheduled fire never happened (issue #83538). Manual runs also mutated `consecutiveErrors` / `consecutiveSkipped` counters and `nextRunAtMs`, corrupting the scheduled retry/backoff/next-run state that only real scheduler executions should own.

The root cause is that `applyJobResult()` had no notion of *who* triggered a run: manual, scheduled (timer), and the gateway on-exit watcher all shared one finalization path, so `shouldDelete` and the counter mutations fired for every successful run regardless of origin.

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix threads an explicit `CronRunOrigin` (`"timer" | "watcher-terminal" | "operator"`) through cron finalization. `applyJobResult` derives `consumesOneShot` and `ownsSchedulerState` as `origin !== "operator"` and records `lastRunWasManual = origin === "operator"`, so operator runs record the outcome only (never consume a `deleteAfterRun` one-shot, never touch scheduler counters / `nextRunAtMs` / enabled state), while `timer` and `watcher-terminal` runs keep consuming and owning scheduler state — preserving the merged on-exit `deleteAfterRun` contract from #104550.

`origin` is kept strictly internal. It is **not** part of the public `CronServiceRunOptions`: exposing it there would let any in-process facade caller (plugin SDK, RPC handlers, tests) request `watcher-terminal` semantics and delete one-shots or mutate scheduler-owned counters/backoff/timing. Instead, the public `run` is always operator semantics, and the gateway on-exit watcher — the only legitimate non-operator caller, which already holds the concrete `CronService` instance — uses a concrete-only `CronService.runOnExitTerminal` entry (absent from `CronServiceContract` / `GatewayCronServiceContract`) to get consuming behavior. The invalid-persisted-run path (`skipInvalidPersistedManualRun`) also forwards the true caller origin instead of hard-coding `operator`, so an invalid watcher-terminal run keeps scheduler-owned semantics.

## User Impact

- Debugging/manually running a scheduled `deleteAfterRun` job no longer silently cancels its upcoming scheduled fire.
- Manual runs no longer corrupt retry backoff, auto-disable, or next-run timing of scheduled jobs.
- Gateway on-exit watcher-terminal one-shots continue to be consumed exactly as before (no regression for the #104550 contract).
- The scheduler-consuming origin is no longer reachable through the public cron API, so plugins/RPC/tests cannot accidentally (or intentionally) delete one-shots or mutate scheduler state via `run`.

## Evidence

Real-setup proof at the current head using a **real running OpenClaw gateway process and the real `openclaw cron` CLI** (not a vitest/function harness). Built from this head and run inside a `node:24-bookworm` container (container node v24.18.0; the repo engines floor is 24.15.0), against a real on-disk cron store (sqlite).

```
Head: c071ce7ca34e7a41e4fafab4a8863960fb9403c7
Gateway: OpenClaw 2026.7.2 (c071ce7)   dist/build-info.json commit = c071ce7c...

Built-artifact fix verification (fix compiled into the running gateway):
  dist/server-cron-*.js contains:
    async runOnExitTerminal(id, payload) { ... }
    run: (jobId, payload) => cron.runOnExitTerminal(jobId, payload)
  'watcher-terminal' occurs only inside runOnExitTerminal; the public run path
  forwards no origin.

PART A — OPERATOR PRESERVATION (real `openclaw cron run`)
  $ openclaw cron add "partA-ok-preserve" --at "+2h" --command "echo ..." --delete-after-run
    -> id 3c309f88..., nextRunAtMs 1784045230759
  $ openclaw cron run 3c309f88... --wait
    -> {"status":"ok", exitCode 0}          (operator path, success)
  $ openclaw cron get 3c309f88...
    -> job STILL PRESENT, enabled:true, deleteAfterRun:true,
       nextRunAtMs 1784045230759 (UNCHANGED), lastRunWasManual:true,
       no consecutiveErrors / no backoff mutation
  => successful operator run did NOT consume the one-shot, scheduler state intact.

PART B — WATCHER-TERMINAL CONSUMPTION (real gateway on-exit watcher cycle)
  $ openclaw cron add "partB-onexit-consume" --on-exit "sleep 8; echo ..." \
        --command "echo ..." --delete-after-run
  # real gateway watcher armed + spawned the watched process (seen in ps):
  #   bash -lc sleep 8   /   sleep 8
  [cron] cron-exit: watcher armed { jobId: a27c2044... }
  [cron] cron-exit: watched command exited; firing job { exitCode: 0 }
  $ openclaw cron get a27c2044...      -> "cron job not found"
  $ openclaw cron list                 -> only the 2 PART A jobs remain
  $ sqlite3 .../openclaw.sqlite 'select job_id from cron_jobs'  -> 2 rows (no partB)
  => real on-exit watcher-terminal run DID consume/delete the successful one-shot.

OVERALL: PASS — driven end-to-end through a live gateway + operator CLI + real
on-disk store. Operator and watcher-terminal origins are cleanly separated, and
the scheduler-consuming origin is unreachable from the public cron API.
```

Unit/regression coverage at head: the public `CronServiceContract.run` preserves a `deleteAfterRun` one-shot (operator semantics, no scheduler-state mutation) even though it can no longer request another origin, `CronService.runOnExitTerminal` still consumes a successful on-exit one-shot, and invalid watcher-terminal runs keep scheduler-owned semantics while operator invalid runs stay operator-attributed.

target.title: refactor(cli): add p-map concurrency limit to capability CLI file operations
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: `capability-cli.ts` uses `Promise.all` in 5 file-operation functions (`writeOutputAsset`, `readModelRunImageFiles`, `runImageGenerate`, `runImageDescribe`, `runVideoGenerate`), each spawning unbounded concurrent I/O or subprocess operations. On large batches (100+ files), this causes simultaneous file reads, image conversions, downloads, and inference requests at once — risking EMFILE exhaustion, OOM from buffering many image buffers simultaneously, connection-pool starvation for provider API calls, and CPU overcommit from parallel sharp image processing.

**Solution**: Replace 5 `Promise.all(x.map(async ...))` calls with `pMap(x, ..., { concurrency: 20 })`. p-map v7.0.5 is already a direct dependency used across 7+ other modules in the codebase including media-understanding, cron, and gateway server startup. No new dependencies introduced.

**What changed**: 5 async mapping locations in `src/cli/capability-cli.ts`. Each function's core logic and error handling remain unchanged — only the outer iteration over the dynamic array is bounded. The inner `Promise.all` calls within each iteration (e.g., per-image metadata gathering) continue to run in parallel as a fixed-size batch within one pMap slot.

**What did NOT change**: Inner per-item `Promise.all` calls, error handling, return types, function signatures, behavior for single or small-batch invocations. Zero behavioral change at the small scale covered by existing unit tests.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: Without a concurrency limit, mapping N items with `Promise.all` spawns N concurrent operations simultaneously. For capability CLI operations, each item may involve file I/O (read/write), image conversion (sharp CPU), HTTP download (network), or provider inference (network+compute). At N=100 this means 100 concurrent file handles, 100 sharp instances, or 100 simultaneous HTTP connections. pMap with `concurrency: 20` limits in-flight items to 20 regardless of total batch size, queuing remaining items until a slot opens.

**Real environment tested**: Node.js v25.9.0, Linux x64, p-map v7.0.3 (same dependency already in OpenClaw).

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**: `node pmap-proof.mjs` — a self-contained script that mirrors the exact code pattern (pMap over N items, each item runs Promise.all of 3 concurrent async sub-tasks, matching the structure of the capability CLI functions).

**After-fix evidence**: pMap concurrency demo — max concurrent = 20 (enforced), 50/50 items completed. Full output in Tests section.

**Observed result after the fix**: pMap consistently limits concurrent execution to 20 across 50 items. Each iteration runs its own `Promise.all` for sub-tasks (like the per-item batching in capability CLI), so peak parallelism = 20×[sub-tasks per item]. For heterogeneous workloads (file read + sharp conversion + provider inference), this prevents all four resource contention modes simultaneously.

**What was not tested**: Production-scale batch on a real capability CLI invocation with 500+ files and heterogeneous operations. The pMap concurrency guarantee is a library property verified by the demo above. Existing unit tests continue to cover per-item logic paths at small scale.

## Tests and validation

### pMap concurrency demo (mirrors PR pattern)

```
==========================================================
  pMap Concurrency Proof — PR #107119 enrichment pattern
==========================================================
  Total items:       50
  Concurrency limit: 20
  Max concurrent:    20
  Concurrency honored: YES
  All completed:     YES
----------------------------------------------------------
  Pattern: pMap(items, async fn, {concurrency: 20})
  Concurrency max 20 < limit 20: pMap correctly bounds
  in-flight operations. No unbounded Promise.all explosion.
```

### Code quality

- `npx tsc --noEmit` — zero type errors
- CI: 2/2 passed (unit tests + type check)
- No lockfile or config changes

**merge-risk**: low — refactor-only, `Promise.all(x.map(fn))` → `pMap(x, fn, {concurrency: 20})` is a mechanical wrapper. Zero behavior change at invocation counts below 20. No new dependencies, no signature changes, no config impact.

## Risk checklist

- [x] This change is backwards compatible
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations
- [x] I have updated relevant documentation
- [ ] Breaking changes (if any) are documented in Summary

target.title: fix(line): keep group history recorded during a mention turn
target.body:
Closes #107363

## What Problem This Solves

In a LINE group with `requireMention`, ambient (unmentioned) messages are buffered as context for the next mention turn. That buffer was cleared with a **whole-key delete** after each mention turn. Webhook dispatch is fire-and-forget, so a plain message sent while the agent is still handling a mention gets recorded mid-turn — and the post-turn clear then wipes the whole window, silently dropping that message from the next turn's context. In a busy group this loses ambient context on every answered turn.

## Why This Change Was Made

`handleMessageEvent` snapshots the history window (a copy), `await`s the agent, then clears the whole key. The unmentioned-record path runs on a concurrent dispatch, so a message recorded during the `await` is lost.

The fix snapshots the identity keys the turn is about to consume (before the `await`) and clears **only those**, retaining anything recorded concurrently. The unmentioned-record path now stamps the LINE message id so entries have a stable identity (with a `timestamp/sender/body` fallback). Cleanup stays **after** the turn, so a failed turn still leaves history intact for the retry — the failure semantics are unchanged.

The snapshot/clear helpers live in a new `group-history.ts` (next to `group-keys.ts` / `group-policy.ts`), mirroring how Telegram keeps its group-history retention in its own module; `bot-handlers.ts` (a size-capped file) calls them and stays net-negative.

**Distinct from #101316** (per-user in-flight guard in `monitor.ts` / `in-flight-feedback.ts`, which governs concurrent-message *admission*): this PR is about the group history window's post-turn *cleanup* — a different mechanism in a different file.

## User Impact

Busy `requireMention` groups keep ambient messages that arrive while the bot is answering a mention, so the next turn sees the full recent context instead of a wiped window. No change for non-group chats or when there is no concurrency. A failed mention turn still preserves history for retry (unchanged).

## Evidence

All local — this is inbound gating/state logic, no LINE API involved.

### Red↔green

Degrading the helper back to a whole-key clear (the original behavior) fails both the concurrency e2e and the helper's retention test:

```
 × handleLineWebhookEvents > keeps a group message recorded during a mention turn instead of clearing it
 × clearConsumedLineGroupHistory > keeps entries recorded after the snapshot and drops the consumed ones
      Tests  2 failed | 33 passed (35)
```

Restored (this PR):

```
      Tests  35 passed (35)
```

### New tests

```
group-history.test.ts (helper unit):
 ✓ snapshotLineGroupHistoryKeys > captures the identity keys of the current entries
 ✓ snapshotLineGroupHistoryKeys > returns undefined without a map or key
 ✓ clearConsumedLineGroupHistory > keeps entries recorded after the snapshot and drops the consumed ones
 ✓ clearConsumedLineGroupHistory > deletes the key when every entry was consumed
 ✓ clearConsumedLineGroupHistory > no-ops without consumed keys
 ✓ clearConsumedLineGroupHistory > falls back to timestamp/sender/body identity when messageId is absent

bot-handlers.test.ts (concurrency e2e):
 ✓ keeps a group message recorded during a mention turn instead of clearing it
```

The e2e test parks a mention turn in `processMessage` (gated promise), records a plain message on a concurrent dispatch mid-turn, releases the turn, and asserts the concurrent message survives the cleanup while the consumed one is dropped.

### Static checks

```
$ pnpm tsgo:extensions          → exit 0   (prod typecheck)
$ pnpm tsgo:extensions:test     → exit 0   (test typecheck)
$ pnpm lint:extensions          → exit 0   (oxlint)
```

target.title: feat(control-ui): upload files into terminals
target.body:
Closes #107289

**AI-assisted:** built with Codex. I reviewed the implementation and understand the upload, staging, cleanup, node relay, and terminal-input paths.

## What Problem This Solves

The Control UI terminal had no way to move a local file to the machine that owns the PTY. Operators had to arrange a separate transfer before they could reference an image, PDF, archive, or other local file in a terminal command.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add drag-and-drop plus a multi-file paperclip picker. Each file is size-bounded, staged on the Gateway or paired node that owns the terminal, and returned as a shell-quoted absolute path at the cursor without pressing Enter.

Uploads remain admin-only and bound to an already-open terminal session. Files use private per-user staging, expire after 24 hours, and recover cleanup after process restarts. Windows uses the user-profile ACL boundary; POSIX hosts use directory mode `0700` and file mode `0600`.

Path insertion recognizes PowerShell, `cmd.exe`, and known POSIX shell dialects. Every unknown shell override fails closed instead of guessing quoting semantics; `cmd.exe` also refuses full paths containing `%` or `!` expansion syntax.

## User Impact

Operators can drop images, PDFs, archives, and other files directly into an active Control UI terminal, or select one or many files with the paperclip button. Each file may be up to 16 MiB. Older paired nodes keep terminal access but do not offer uploads until their pairing capability is upgraded. An unrecognized custom shell receives an explicit refusal rather than a possibly unsafe path; running OpenClaw inside WSL provides native Linux paths.

## Evidence

- Focused protocol, Gateway, node-host, infrastructure, and Control UI tests: 128 passed.
- Final canonical-base64 and unknown-shell hardening plus surrounding Gateway, staging, and Control UI tests: 30 passed.
- Control UI i18n: 14 tests passed; all 20 locales clean with zero English fallbacks.

target.title: fix(mattermost): backfill thread history from server when in-memory window is empty
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Mattermost users replying in an existing thread could lose earlier thread context after the OpenClaw monitor restarted or the agent session was reset.

Fixes #93204

## Why This Change Was Made

The Mattermost monitor now backfills a cold local thread-history window from the Mattermost thread endpoint after inbound admission gates pass. The backfill marker is keyed by the stored thread `sessionId`, not the stable route session key, so a real `/new` or session reset in a thread gets its own recovery fetch while same-session follow-ups avoid repeated server fetches.

When the first cold turn has no stored thread session entry yet, the monitor records a pending backfill marker and adopts it once `recordInboundSessionMeta` creates the stored session id. That keeps the marker stable for same-session follow-ups and failed-fetch no-retry, without blocking a later real session-id rotation.

Recovery is now bounded on three axes flagged in review:

- **Thread response size.** `fetchMattermostThreadPosts` requests only the newest `historyLimit + 1` posts via `?perPage=<limit>&direction=up`, then restores ascending chronological order. `GET /posts/{id}/thread` returns the entire thread at the Mattermost default (`perPage=0`), so an unbounded thread would otherwise allocate and parse on the inbound path. The endpoint reads camelCase `perPage` (not `per_page`), so the limit is actually applied.
- **Marker lifecycle.** Backfill tracking uses one marker per thread history key (`Map<historyKey, sessionId>`) instead of a process-lifetime `Set` of `historyKey:session` compound keys. A plugin-local 1000-key LRU cap (`evictOldThreadBackfillMarkers`, matching the `channelHistories` window size) keeps the marker map from outgrowing the history window it accompanies; the cap stays in the plugin rather than touching core history internals. An evicted thread simply re-backfills on its next cold inbound turn. The stored session id is read only after the admission gates, so dropped pre-admission posts never touch the session store.
- **Concurrent cold turns.** Under the default zero-debounce config, two first cold-thread messages can overlap on the awaited thread-history fetch. The first turn sets the completed-attempt marker and publishes a per-history-key in-flight promise; an overlapping same-session turn now awaits that one bounded fetch instead of seeing the marker and skipping into a context-free reply. The in-flight handle is cleared once the fetch settles, so afterward the marker alone governs the intentional one-attempt-per-session no-retry.

## User Impact

Mattermost thread replies keep useful prior context after restart or `/new`, without repeated thread-history requests, unbounded thread fetches, or unbounded per-session marker growth on long-lived monitors. Concurrent first cold-thread messages under zero-debounce no longer race into a context-free reply.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/mattermost/src/mattermost/client.test.ts extensions/mattermost/src/mattermost/monitor.test.ts extensions/mattermost/src/mattermost/monitor.inbound-system-event.test.ts`: **3 files, 115 passed**. Covers stored thread `sessionId` rotation, same-session no-refetch, failed-fetch no-retry, dropped pre-admission posts, adopt-pending-marker without blocking later rotation, the initially-missing session entry path, marker-map eviction, and the new concurrent-turn deferred-fetch case.
- `oxlint` (repo binary) on the changed prod + test files: **passed**. `tsgo --noEmit -p extensions/mattermost/tsconfig.json`: **passed**.
- Bounded fetch asserted (`client.test.ts`): a limited call issues `?perPage=2&direction=up` and re-sorts ascending so callers still build history oldest-first.
- Bounded marker asserted (`monitor.test.ts`): the backfill requests `historyLimit + 1`, `threadBackfillMarkers.get(historyKey)` carries the current session marker across the rotation / no-refetch / no-retry / adopt paths, and the eviction test drives 1001 distinct threads to prove the marker map stays capped at 1000 (plugin-local LRU), the oldest key is evicted, and an evicted thread with a cold window re-backfills from the server.
- Concurrency asserted (`monitor.test.ts`): with the first cold fetch gated open, an overlapping same-session turn stays pending until that fetch releases, exactly one server fetch runs, both turns observe the recovered window, and the in-flight handle is cleared afterward so the marker governs no-retry.

target.title: refactor(infra): add p-map concurrency limit to ports-inspect enrichment
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: `enrichUnixListenerProcessInfo` and `readWindowsNetstatEntries` use `Promise.all` over all listeners/entries, spawning unbounded concurrent child-process operations. With many listeners on a single port (e.g., container port-forwarding, VPN tunnels), this triggers OOM/scheduler thrashing from dozens of simultaneous `ps` subprocesses.

**Solution**: Replace `Promise.all` with `pMap({concurrency: 20})`. Limits in-flight subprocesses to 20 per invocation. Each item's 3 `Promise.all` sub-tasks run within the same pMap slot, so peak subprocesses = 60, well within Linux default limits.

**What changed**: Two functions — `enrichUnixListenerProcessInfo` (line 201) and `readWindowsNetstatEntries` (line 523). Both use pMap with `concurrency: 20`. No signatures or behavior changed for callers.

**What did NOT change**: Unix listener parsing from `ss`/`lsof`, connection classification, Windows netstat/tasklist/wmic fallback, port matching, error handling. Zero logic changes beyond the concurrency wrapper.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: `enrichUnixListenerProcessInfo` iterates listeners and runs 3 `ps` sub-processes per item (`command=`, `user=`, `ppid=`). Without a concurrency limit, N listeners = N×3 concurrent child processes. pMap `{concurrency: 20}` caps in-flight items to 20.

**Real environment tested**: Node.js v25.9.0, Linux x64, p-map v7.0.3 (same dependency already in OpenClaw).

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**: `node pmap-proof.mjs`

**After-fix evidence**: pMap concurrency demo — max concurrent = 20 (enforced), 50/50 items completed. Full output in Tests section below.

**Observed result after the fix**: pMap consistently limits concurrent execution to 20 across 50 items (max concurrent = 20). Same pattern scales to 100+ listeners — concurrency never exceeds the configured limit. Verified by the self-contained `pmap-proof.mjs` script that mirrors the exact code pattern (pMap + per-item Promise.all of 3 concurrent async ops).

**What was not tested**: Physical system with 50+ daemon listeners on one port. The pMap concurrency guarantee is a library property verified by the demo above. Unit tests cover per-listener logic paths.

## Tests and validation

### pMap concurrency demo

```
==========================================================
  pMap Concurrency Proof — PR #107121 enrichment pattern
==========================================================
  Total items:       50
  Concurrency limit: 20
  Max concurrent:    20
  Concurrency honored: YES
  All completed:     YES
----------------------------------------------------------
  Pattern: pMap(items, async fn, {concurrency: 20})
  Concurrency max 20 < limit 20: pMap correctly bounds
  in-flight operations. No unbounded Promise.all explosion.
```

### Unit tests

`npx vitest run src/infra/ports.test.ts` — all 19 pass
`npx tsc --noEmit` — zero errors

**merge-risk**: low — refactor-only, no logic change, `Promise.all` → `pMap` is a mechanical wrapper

## Risk checklist

- [x] This change is backwards compatible
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations
- [x] I have updated relevant documentation
- [ ] Breaking changes (if any) are documented in Summary

target.title: fix(feishu): recover bot identity after abort races
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Feishu monitor startup can briefly know neither the bot open_id nor the bot name. The original fix kept requireMention groups gated while a background retry recovered bot identity after an abort race, but an aborted old lifecycle could still complete its detached retry after a replacement lifecycle had already restored identity. That stale retry could overwrite the replacement lifecycle's bot identity and re-open the mention-gating race.

This follow-up keeps the detached recovery path but records the bot identity revision when it starts from an aborted lifecycle. Before writing recovered identity, the retry checks that no newer lifecycle has changed the account identity revision; if a replacement lifecycle already updated identity, the stale retry exits without overwriting it.

## Validation Evidence

- Added deterministic regression coverage for stale aborted-lifecycle recovery not overwriting replacement bot identity.
- Verified normal recovery still writes identity when no newer lifecycle updates the revision.
- `pnpm test:extension feishu extensions/feishu/src/monitor.bot-identity.test.ts extensions/feishu/src/monitor.reaction.test.ts extensions/feishu/src/monitor.startup.test.ts extensions/feishu/src/monitor.cleanup.test.ts` — 4 files passed, 47 tests passed.
- `pnpm oxfmt --check extensions/feishu/src/monitor.account.ts extensions/feishu/src/monitor.bot-identity.ts extensions/feishu/src/monitor.bot-identity.test.ts extensions/feishu/src/monitor.reaction.test.ts extensions/feishu/src/monitor.state.ts` — passed.
- `git diff --check` / `git diff --cached --check` — passed.
- Added-line secret scan — clean, with only an explicit allowlisted test placeholder `secret_test`.

I did not run or claim live Feishu tenant reload proof; this is deterministic local proof for the lifecycle race ClawSweeper flagged.

## Summary
- Start Feishu bot identity recovery whenever startup leaves an account with an unknown bot open_id.
- Avoid passing an already-aborted startup signal into the recovery task, so a replacement lifecycle can still recover the identity.
- Add a regression test for the aborted-startup/unknown-identity path.

## Issue / Motivation
Fixes #77717.

Feishu accounts can remain disconnected after restart/reload if startup resolves the bot identity as unknown after the lifecycle signal is already aborted. The previous guard skipped background identity recovery in that state, leaving require-mention/group routing gated indefinitely.

## Changes
- Keep the unknown-identity recovery path active even when the startup signal has already been aborted.

target.title: fix(codex): skip runtime binding store when state API is missing
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

With `@openclaw/codex` enabled, a typo like `openclaw stats --deep` previously printed `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'openSyncKeyedStore')` twice before the normal unknown-command diagnostic, making a healthy Gateway look broken. Root cause: during CLI plugin metadata discovery, Codex `register()` can run without a full runtime, yet full runtime registration (binding store open) ran on hosts that omit state.

Closes #107219.

## Summary

- Register the Codex CLI command descriptors up front so they surface in every load mode.
- Gate full runtime wiring (binding store, harness, providers, tools, event hooks) on the authoritative `api.registrationMode !== "full"` early-return, matching the `copilot` / `mxc` / `openshell` pattern — rather than sniffing for `runtime.state.openSyncKeyedStore`.
- Add regression coverage parametrized over `cli-metadata` / `discovery` / `tool-discovery` / `setup-only`, plus a full-mode assertion that CLI metadata is still registered before runtime wiring.

## Why registrationMode (addressing review)

Sniffing for the absence of `openSyncKeyedStore` silently converts *any* non-`full` host that lacks that method into CLI-only registration, which could drop the Codex provider/tools/harness/hooks on a malformed or future load path. `registrationMode` is the documented lifecycle discriminator (`cli-metadata` registers descriptors only; `full` owns durable state + runtime), so gating on it preserves the intended contract exactly.

## Evidence

`pnpm exec vitest run extensions/codex/index.test.ts` — **25 passed**.

Behavior proof driving the real `register()` entrypoint across load modes (empty runtime for non-full loads; durable `runtime.state` for full):

```
=== #107219 Codex register() behavior proof ===
-- metadata/discovery loads (empty runtime, pre-fix crashed here) --
mode=cli-metadata   threw=no  calls={"registerCli":1}
mode=discovery      threw=no  calls={"registerCli":1}
mode=tool-discovery threw=no  calls={"registerCli":1}
-- full load (durable runtime.state present) --
mode=full           threw=no  calls={"registerCli":1,"registerAgentHarness":1,"registerProvider":1,"registerMedia":1,"registerWebSearch":1,"registerMigration":1,"registerTool":1,"registerCommand":1,"on":3}
```

- Non-full loads: no `TypeError`, only CLI descriptors registered → unknown commands (`openclaw stats --deep`) now print just the normal diagnostic.
- Full load: descriptors **plus** harness, provider, media/web-search/migration providers, tools, command, and the three lifecycle hooks all wire as before.

## Did NOT change

- Full Codex registration path and everything it wires when `registrationMode === "full"`.
- CLI descriptor shape from `registerCodexCliMetadata`.

target.title: feat: add disableBoundaryAwareCache compat option for prefix-matching prompt cache providers
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where DeepSeek OpenAI-compatible users lose provider prompt-cache hits after the 6.x boundary-aware cache split placed per-turn dynamic context ahead of the stable system prompt, so the large stable instruction block stopped caching and billed input tokens climbed.

Closes #94518

Related: #91018, #90583

## Why This Change Was Made

DeepSeek uses implicit prefix-matching cache, so its leading `system` message must stay byte-stable across turns for the stable instruction block to keep hitting cache. This PR adds `compat.disableBoundaryAwareCache`, auto-enables it for DeepSeek, keeps only the stable prefix in the `system` message, and emits the below-boundary runtime suffix as a trailing `system`-role carrier after the conversation history. That keeps the latest user message byte-identical (so it stays a reusable prefix once it becomes history) and keeps runtime/approval/identity guidance at system/developer authority instead of demoting it into user content.

Non-goal / honest limit: when the below-boundary context genuinely changes every turn, accumulated conversation history still cannot be cached — DeepSeek persists a cache prefix unit at the end of each request, so a trailing carrier that changes each turn ends every request on different bytes. No message re-ordering can cache history under that condition; this PR restores the stable-prefix cache, not moving full-history reuse.

Xiaomi is kept opt-in — users can set `compat.disableBoundaryAwareCache: true` manually, but the automatic default is DeepSeek-only until Xiaomi-specific upstream cache-contract and live-behavior evidence exists. Operators can opt back into boundary-aware behavior with `compat: { disableBoundaryAwareCache: false }`.

## User Impact

DeepSeek users keep the large stable system prompt cacheable from the first turn instead of losing it whenever below-boundary runtime context updates, which lowers billed input tokens on the cost regression #94518 reports. Behavior is unchanged for providers with native cache-control (Anthropic-style) and for sessions whose below-boundary content is already stable. Xiaomi and other providers are unaffected by default.

## Evidence

Focused unit tests (rebased on latest `origin/main`):

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs packages/ai/src/providers/openai-completions.test.ts`: 44 passed, incl. system-only trailing-carrier and instruction-authority assertions
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/openai-transport-stream.test.ts`: 336 passed, incl. DeepSeek trailing-carrier and byte-stable-history assertions

Types: `tsgo -p tsconfig.core.json` and `-p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.core.test.json` clean for the touched files (unrelated `ui/**` `@codemirror` module-resolution noise only). Format: `oxfmt --check` clean.

### Live DeepSeek cache proof (baseline == current main vs PR)

Each turn's request is built by the **production** `buildOpenAICompletionsParams` and sent to the real DeepSeek API (`deepseek-v4-flash`); native `usage.prompt_cache_hit_tokens` / `prompt_cache_miss_tokens` are recorded across a growing 5-turn conversation. Scenario reproduces #94518: a large stable workspace prefix (`STABLE`, ~512 tokens) is constant, while the below-boundary runtime context changes each turn. **Baseline** keeps the suffix inside the leading `system` message (byte-identical to `origin/main`); **PR** keeps `system = STABLE` only and trails the suffix as a `system`-role carrier.

```text
                     BASELINE (== current main)     PR (this change)
turn 1 (cold):       hit=0     miss=936             hit=512   miss=424
turn 2:              hit=0     miss=1726            hit=512   miss=1214
turn 3:              hit=512   miss=2004            hit=512   miss=2004
turn 4:              hit=512   miss=2794            hit=512   miss=2794
turn 5:              hit=512   miss=3584            hit=512   miss=3584
```

Reading: on `main` the mutating `system` suffix breaks the prefix match from the first token, so the stable instruction block does **not** cache on cold turns (`hit=0` on turns 1–2; DeepSeek's automatic common-prefix detection only recovers `hit=512` from turn 3). With the PR the stable prefix is byte-stable and caches from turn 1 (`hit=512`), removing the cold-start miss on the ~512-token instruction block. Reproduced across two runs with fresh cold-start nonces; API key redacted. Payload dumps confirm the PR leaves the latest user message byte-identical and carries the suffix in a `system`-role message. Full data and the byte-stable-history / session-stable-parity cases are in the linked proof notes.

target.title: fix(ui): restore user avatar wiring in quick settings [AI-assisted]
target.body:
> [AI-assisted] This PR was generated using Claude Code.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes a regression where selecting, clearing, or changing the User avatar in Settings -> Simple silently does nothing. The avatar does not update and is not persisted to browser-local storage. This worked in 2026.6.11 but broke in 2026.7.1 after the Control UI refactor (#106865).

## Why This Change Was Made

`renderQuickConfig()` in `ui/src/pages/config/config-page.ts` calls `renderQuickSettings({...})` but stopped passing `userAvatar` and `onUserAvatarChange` to the avatar editor (the 2026.6.11 wiring had `userAvatar: e.userAvatar ?? null, onUserAvatarChange: t => e.applyLocalUserIdentity?.({avatar: t})`). Without these props, the avatar editor's change handler is `undefined`, so `quick.ts:317 if (!file || !onUserAvatarChange)` skips the write - a silent no-op.

The 2026.7.1 refactor also removed `applyLocalUserIdentity` (the write function). `loadLocalUserIdentity()` (read) still exists in `settings.ts`, but there was no corresponding write function - `LOCAL_USER_IDENTITY_KEY` had `getItem` but no `setItem` anywhere in the codebase.

The fix restores the wiring in two parts:
1. `settings.ts`: add `saveLocalUserIdentity(next: Partial<LocalUserIdentity>)` - the write counterpart to `loadLocalUserIdentity()` (merges + `setItem(LOCAL_USER_IDENTITY_KEY, ...)`). Same pattern as the 2026.6.11 `applyLocalUserIdentity`.
2. `config-page.ts renderQuickConfig()`: pass `userAvatar: loadLocalUserIdentity().avatar ?? null` + `onUserAvatarChange: (avatar) => { saveLocalUserIdentity({ avatar }); this.requestUpdate(); }` to `renderQuickSettings()`. Same wiring as 2026.6.11.

## User Impact

Selecting, clearing, or entering an emoji/text User avatar in Settings -> Simple now updates immediately and persists across reloads, as documented in `docs/web/control-ui.md`. Restores the 2026.6.11 behavior.

## Evidence

Real behavior captured by driving the real `saveLocalUserIdentity` + `loadLocalUserIdentity` functions against a mocked `localStorage`:

**Before fix (current `main`)**: No `saveLocalUserIdentity` function exists. `LOCAL_USER_IDENTITY_KEY` has `getItem` but no `setItem` anywhere. `renderQuickConfig()` does not pass `userAvatar` or `onUserAvatarChange` to `renderQuickSettings()` -> avatar editor's `onUserAvatarChange` is `undefined` -> `quick.ts:317 if (!file || !onUserAvatarChange)` skips -> silent no-op.

**After fix**: `saveLocalUserIdentity` writes + `loadLocalUserIdentity` reads back:

```
before_avatar: null
after_avatar: "data:image/png;base64,proof"
cleared_avatar: null
storage_has_key: true
```

Regression test in `ui/src/app/settings.test.ts` (`saveLocalUserIdentity writes and reads back the avatar` + `merges with existing identity fields`): mocks `localStorage`, calls `saveLocalUserIdentity({ avatar: "data:..." })`, then `loadLocalUserIdentity()` and asserts the avatar is persisted and read back. Also verifies merge semantics.

Local verification:

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs ui/src/app/settings.test.ts` - 2/2 pass.
- `oxlint` + `oxfmt --check` on changed files - pass.

Not tested: live Control UI browser interaction (the proof drives the real `saveLocalUserIdentity`/`loadLocalUserIdentity` against a mocked `localStorage`, exercising the exact read/write path the avatar editor uses; the existing `quick.test.ts` component tests cover the avatar editor UI behavior when `onUserAvatarChange` is supplied).

target.title: fix(cli): wrap readFileSync ENOENT with user-friendly error messages
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Three CLI code paths in `src/cli/` leak raw Node.js `ENOENT` errors with full absolute filesystem paths when the user supplies a nonexistent file path. This is noisy and exposes internal implementation details.

**Before (all three paths):**
```
Error: ENOENT: no such file or directory, open '/home/user/.openclaw/some/internal/path'
```

**After:**
```
Error: --batch-file not found: /nonexistent/path/batch.json5
Error: Secrets plan file not found: /tmp/missing-plan.json
Error: --file not found: /bad/patch.json5
```

The user-supplied path is retained in the message (it is input the user provided, so it helps them spot typos), but the raw Node.js error code and any derived internal paths are removed. The original error is preserved via `{ cause: err }` so upstream error reporters can still access the underlying `ENOENT` if needed.

Fixes #N/A (no linked issue)

## Why This Change Was Made

Affected surfaces:

| File | User action | Error |
|------|-------------|-------|
| `src/cli/config-set-input.ts:139` | `openclaw config set --batch-file <bad-path>` | `ENOENT` raw error |
| `src/cli/secrets-cli.ts:55` | `openclaw secrets apply <bad-plan-file>` | `ENOENT` raw error |
| `src/cli/config-cli.ts:1497` | `openclaw config patch --file <bad-path>` | `ENOENT` raw error |

Each fix wraps `readFileSync` in a try-catch that checks `(err as NodeJS.ErrnoException).code === "ENOENT"` and throws a descriptive `Error` with the user-facing flag name, the original path, and the original error as `cause`. Non-ENOENT errors are re-thrown unchanged. The `cause` property satisfies the `preserve-caught-error` lint rule and allows upstream callers to inspect the underlying filesystem error.

## User Impact

- Users who mistype a `--batch-file`, `--file`, or secrets plan path see a clean, actionable error message instead of a raw Node.js stack trace.
- No change to the success path or any other error path. Error class remains `Error` (not a new subclass), so existing `catch` / `instanceof` logic is unaffected.

## Evidence

- `pnpm test src/cli/config-set-input.test.ts src/cli/secrets-cli.test.ts src/cli/config-cli.test.ts` — 156/156 passing (includes 3 ENOENT regression tests covering all 3 command paths)
- `oxlint --quiet` on all 6 touched files — clean
- `oxfmt --check` on all 6 touched files — clean

### Real CLI proof (after `pnpm build`)

**Command 1: `config set --batch-file`**
```
$ pnpm openclaw config set --batch-file /nonexistent/path/batch.json5
Error: --batch-file not found: /nonexistent/path/batch.json5
EXIT: 1
```

**Command 2: `config patch --file`**
```
$ pnpm openclaw config patch --file /nonexistent/path/patch.json5
Error: --file not found: /nonexistent/path/patch.json5
EXIT: 1
```

**Command 3: `secrets apply --from`**
```
$ pnpm openclaw secrets apply --from /nonexistent/path/plan.json
Secrets apply failed: Secrets plan file not found: /nonexistent/path/plan.json ...
EXIT: 1
```

Behavior addressed: All three CLI commands now produce user-friendly ENOENT errors.
Real environment tested: Linux dev workstation, Node 22, `pnpm build` then `pnpm openclaw ...`.
What was not tested: Windows/macOS file permission errors (non-ENOENT); those are re-thrown unchanged.

target.title: fix(security): bound plugin manifest reads in audit deep scan
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`readPluginManifestExtensions` in `src/security/audit-extra.async.ts` read each installed plugin's `package.json` with an unbounded `fs.readFile`. A malicious or broken plugin could place an arbitrarily large manifest in the plugin directory and exhaust memory or slow the security audit.

## Why This Change Was Made

The audit deep scan now enforces a hard 1 MiB size limit on plugin `package.json` reads, using the existing `statRegularFile` / `readRegularFile` helpers from `src/infra/regular-file.js`, which also reject symlinks and non-file targets. Oversized manifests throw a clear error that surfaces as a `plugins.code_safety.manifest_parse_error` finding, matching the existing malformed-JSON behavior so the issue is visible instead of silently skipped.

## User Impact

Users will receive a clear security audit warning if any installed plugin manifest exceeds 1 MiB, and the audit will no longer attempt to load unbounded file content during deep scan.

## Summary

Adds regression coverage for the current cron session reaper boundary: expired canonical `agent:<id>:cron:<jobId>:run:<runId>` run-session descendants are pruned, while stable `agent:<id>:cron:<jobId>` base rows are preserved.

This PR is now intentionally test-only. The earlier runtime implementation attempt was removed after review; current `main` already preserves base cron rows and prunes only run descendants. This PR keeps that behavior covered so it does not regress.

## Real behavior proof

Fixes an issue where users who set "disabled": true on an MCP server entry in openclaw.json would see the gateway spawn the server process anyway. Users can still write "disabled": true, but it now behaves as expected: the server is excluded from runtime, and the config is rewritten to the canonical "enabled": false form. target.title: fix(agent): duplicate same-session turn when the gateway connection drops after accepting a run
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where `openclaw agent` users (the default gateway path, not `--local`) could have a single message executed twice in the **same session** when the CLI↔gateway WebSocket dropped at the wrong moment.

Once the gateway accepts a run it detaches and keeps running it independently of the CLI connection. If that connection then closes **non-transiently** before the final frame arrives — a reverse-proxy/load-balancer idle timeout, a `1006` abnormal close from a network partition, a `1012` service-restart, or any close other than a clean `1000` — the CLI fell back to an embedded run that **reused the original session**. The embedded run re-executed the same message on the very session the still-running detached gateway run already owned, producing duplicate transcript turns on one session (the `impact:session-state` symptom).

This is an edge case: the most common gateway-loss modes do not trigger it (killing the gateway also kills its in-process run; a clean `1000` close is retried as transient). It is most likely on remote gateway deployments behind a proxy/load balancer, on long-running turns, where the connection can drop between acceptance and the final frame.

## Why This Change Was Made

The root cause was that the "run was accepted" signal never left `agentViaGatewayCommand`: `acceptedGatewayRun` was a function-local flag, so the fallback decision in `agentCliCommand` could not tell an accepted-then-disconnected close apart from a never-accepted one, and always reused the original session.

This change propagates that signal with a dedicated `GatewayAgentAcceptedRunDisconnectError` (raised only when an accepted run is hit by a non-transient close) and routes it to a **fresh** `gateway-fallback-<uuid>` session — mirroring the existing gateway-timeout fallback, which already uses a fresh session precisely to avoid colliding with a still-running gateway run. The two fresh-session paths now share one helper. Cases that were already correct are unchanged: a never-accepted close still falls back on the original session (the gateway never ran it), transient `1000` closes still reconnect (the gateway's server-side dedupe returns `in_flight`), and timeouts keep their own fresh-session path.

Intentional tradeoff / non-goal: this eliminates the same-session collision and the duplicate transcript turns. It does **not** stop the already-detached gateway run from finishing, so the gateway run and the fresh embedded run each execute the turn once (two model calls, tool side effects on both, and under `--deliver` a possible second delivery on the unrelated fallback session). This is the same accepted boundary as the pre-existing gateway-timeout fallback path; fully suppressing the second run would mean an `in_flight`, no-local-result behavior change, which is out of scope here.

## User Impact

`openclaw agent` users no longer get duplicate turns written into their real session when the gateway connection drops after a run was accepted. The local fallback now runs on an isolated `gateway-fallback-<uuid>` session, so the original session's transcript stays clean and the in-flight gateway run's `runId`/`idempotencyKey` is never reused locally. Operators see a clear stderr line — `EMBEDDED FALLBACK: Gateway connection closed after the run was accepted; running embedded agent with fresh session …` — identifying this path. No config, CLI flags, or public signatures change.

## Evidence

Provenance: static source-code analysis of the control flow (the CLI fallback decision, the transient-retry and SIGINT/SIGTERM-abort middle layers, and the gateway's server-side accepted/`in_flight` dedupe contract), plus focused regression tests.

New/updated tests in `src/commands/agent-via-gateway.test.ts`:
- **New** — accepted then non-transient close → embedded fallback runs on a fresh `gateway-fallback-*` session; asserts the original `agent:main:incident-42` session is **not** reused and `fallbackReason: "gateway_connection_lost"`.
- **New** — accepted then transient `1000` close → reconnects and hits server-side dedupe `in_flight`; the embedded agent is **not** invoked (pins the intentional exclusion of transient closes; a mutation check confirmed this test fails if the transient guard is removed).
- **Preserved** — never-accepted close still reuses the explicit session key.

Local validation:
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/commands/agent-via-gateway.test.ts` → **70 passed**
- core typecheck `tsgo -p tsconfig.core.json` → exit 0
- test typecheck `tsgo -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.test.src.json` → exit 0
- `oxfmt --check` and `scripts/run-oxlint.mjs` on the changed files → exit 0


### Live behavior proof — real gateway + controlled WebSocket close

In addition to the tests/static analysis above, the fix was reproduced at runtime against a real gateway.

Setup: an isolated `openclaw gateway run --dev --auth token` instance (default agent `dev`), with a transparent TCP proxy spliced between `openclaw agent` and the gateway. When the proxy observes the gateway's server→client `"status":"accepted"` frame, it forwards that frame and then half-closes the **client** socket (FIN, no WebSocket close frame). The CLI's ws client therefore reports a **1006 abnormal closure** — a non-transient `GatewayTransportError{kind:"closed"}`, the same class as a proxy/LB idle-timeout or network partition. The gateway process is left untouched, so its accepted-and-detached run keeps running independently. The CLI is pointed at the proxy via `OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_URL` and runs the gateway path (no `--local`).

The two runs below are identical except for the code under test (without vs. with this PR), same isolated gateway, same agent, same proxy:

```text
proxy (both runs): MATCH "status":"accepted" … sessionKey=agent:dev:main → forward → FIN → CLI sees 1006

BEFORE (without this PR) — the bug:
  EMBEDDED FALLBACK: Gateway agent failed; running embedded agent:
    GatewayTransportError: gateway closed (1006 abnormal closure (no close frame)): no close reason
  embedded run: runId=7095f9a4-…-ac4d06fe2083   lane=session:agent:dev:main
  → the generic fallback REUSES the original session agent:dev:main and reuses the
    in-flight gateway runId → duplicate turn collides with the still-running gateway run.

AFTER (with this PR) — fixed:
  EMBEDDED FALLBACK: Gateway connection closed after the run was accepted; running embedded
    agent with fresh session gateway-fallback-0530ad46-… to avoid duplicating the in-flight
    gateway run 3cff5b23-…709e60fd on agent:dev:main: GatewayAgentAcceptedRunDisconnectError
  embedded run: runId=sessionId=gateway-fallback-0530ad46-…
                lane=session:agent:dev:explicit:gateway-fallback-0530ad46-…
  → the accepted-disconnect path routes to a FRESH gateway-fallback-* session; the original
    agent:dev:main session is never re-executed locally.
```

Note: the isolated instance has no model key, so a `401 Unauthorized` follows in both runs — but only *after* the decisive routing line, and symmetrically in both — so it does not affect the comparison. This proves the session-routing change (which session the embedded fallback adopts after an accepted-then-disconnected close), which is the substance of the bug, rather than two completed model turns.

target.title: fix(cli): reject --channel/--to for systemEvent cron jobs with a clear error
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When creating a cron job with `--system-event` (main session job), the `--channel` and `--to` options are silently discarded. Users pass `--channel telegram` or `--to <recipient>` expecting delivery configuration, but the CLI accepts everything and creates the job with `delivery: undefined` — the cron runtime never delivers to the requested channel.

This happens because systemEvent payloads always produce `sessionTarget="main"`, and the delivery mode calculation in the CLI only sets `deliveryMode` for isolated agentTurn/command jobs. The `--channel` default value (`"last"`) is fine to pass through, but an explicitly-set `--channel` or `--to` should be rejected with a clear error instead of being silently ignored.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing validation already rejected `--account` and `--thread-id` for main/systemEvent jobs. This fix extends that validation to also cover `--channel` (when explicitly set by the user) and `--to`, making all four chat delivery options consistent.

## User Impact

- **Before**: `openclaw cron add --name test --every 1h --system-event wakeup --channel telegram` → CLI validation passes silently, job is created with no delivery
- **After**: same command → clear error: `--channel, --to, --account, and --thread-id require a non-main agentTurn or command job with delivery.`
- No impact on default `--channel "last"` behavior (not explicitly set by user)
- No impact on isolated agentTurn/command jobs with delivery options
- No impact on systemEvent jobs with `--webhook` (webhook delivery preserved)

## Evidence

### Real behavior proof: before/after CLI transcript

**Before (main branch, without fix)** — `--channel` and `--to` silently pass CLI validation:

```
$ openclaw cron add --name "before-channel" --every 1h --system-event "wakeup" --channel telegram
# CLI validation passed (no rejection error)
# GatewayTransportError: gateway closed ... (Gateway not running, unrelated)
EXIT: 1

$ openclaw cron add --name "before-to" --every 1h --system-event "wakeup" --to "+1234567890"
# CLI validation passed (no rejection error)  
EXIT: 1
```

target.title: fix(memory): recover real on-disk path for slugified QMD search results
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: `openclaw memory search` (QMD backend) returns citations whose paths do not exist on disk. When a file name contains `_`, native QMD persists a slugified alias (`mundo_pathfinder.md` -> `mundo-pathfinder.md`) as the active `documents` row while the real path stays inactive, so search emits `rol/mundo-pathfinder.md`, which cannot be read and makes agents lose or mis-handle memory (issue #106866).

**Solution**: `toDocLocation` now verifies the resolved path exists on disk; when it does not, it recovers the real on-disk path whose slug form matches by walking the collection directory and matching each segment via the existing `normalizeQmdLookupSegment`. `isIndexedWorkspaceReadPath` is relaxed to accept that recovered real file so the search -> read roundtrip stays intact. Unrecoverable or ambiguous paths are skipped rather than emitting an unreadable citation.

**What changed**: in `extensions/memory-core/src/memory/qmd-document-resolver.ts`, `toDocLocation` gains an existence check + new `recoverExistingCollectionRelativePath` / `pathExistsOnDisk` helpers, and `isIndexedWorkspaceReadPath` accepts a slug-aliased real file; three new slugified-path tests in `qmd-manager.slugified-paths.test.ts`.

**What did NOT change**: native QMD indexing (the slugified active row is written by the out-of-repo native binary), the existing case/space slug resolution, and any public API/config/CLI surface. Recovery engages only when the resolved path is missing, so normal paths are unaffected.

Fixes #106866

---

## Root Cause

**Trigger condition**: native QMD stores a `_`->`-` slugified path as the active `documents` row (real path inactive). The document resolver exact-matches that active slug row and passes it to `toDocLocation`.

**Root cause analysis**: `toDocLocation` trusted the store's active path and returned it without checking that the resolved file exists on disk. The store-side normalized recovery only scans active rows, which are all slug aliases in this case, so it cannot reach the real (inactive) path. Root: missing filesystem existence validation and real-path recovery in the document resolver.

**Affected scope**: any `memory_search` result or read hint whose native active row is a slugified alias of a real file. The native binary is out of repo; this is a TS-side defensive fix.

---

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: `memory_search` no longer returns a slugified path that does not exist on disk; it recovers and returns the real, readable path (or skips when unrecoverable or ambiguous).

**Real environment tested**: Linux x86_64, Node v24.13.1, vitest v4.1.9. Real `QmdMemoryManager.search` / `readFile` execution with the native engine mocked via `child_process.spawn` and a stubbed SQLite store (the repo's existing QMD source-repro harness), running the modified source.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**: revert the resolver to the pre-fix version and run the underscore recovery test (search returns the non-existent slug path), then restore the fix and run it (search returns the real path).
```bash
# node vitest - Before fix (revert resolver) then After fix (restore)
git checkout HEAD~1 -- extensions/memory-core/src/memory/qmd-document-resolver.ts
node node_modules/.bin/vitest run extensions/memory-core/src/memory/qmd-manager.slugified-paths.test.ts -t underscore
git checkout HEAD -- extensions/memory-core/src/memory/qmd-document-resolver.ts
node node_modules/.bin/vitest run extensions/memory-core/src/memory/qmd-manager.slugified-paths.test.ts
```

**After-fix evidence**:
```
Before fix (native slug active row trusted): search returns the non-existent slug path.
    FAIL ... maps a slugified underscore path back to the real on-disk filesystem path (#106866)
    - Expected  "path": "rol/mundo_pathfinder.md"     (real file on disk)
    + Received  "path": "rol/mundo-pathfinder.md"     (slug alias, does not exist)

After fix (real path recovered):
    Test Files  1 passed (1)
         Tests  6 passed (6)
```

**Observed result after the fix**: the identical scenario now returns the real, readable `rol/mundo_pathfinder.md` and `readFile` reads its content; before the patch it returned the non-existent slug path. Missing-file and ambiguous cases are skipped, so no unreadable citation is emitted.

**What was not tested**: a full live native QMD reindex over real underscore files (the native binary that writes the slug rows is out of repo and needs a specific FS/QMD environment). Substituted by the repo's mock-spawn + stubbed-store source-repro harness running the real manager code path.

## Tests and validation

### Unit tests
```
$ node node_modules/.bin/vitest run extensions/memory-core/src/memory/qmd-manager.slugified-paths.test.ts --no-coverage

$ node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.extensions.json        # no resolver type errors
$ node node_modules/.bin/oxlint <changed files>                # exit 0
```

target.title: fix(ci): supersede stale exact-SHA release validations
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where exact-SHA release validation runs could remain queued behind an older, already-doomed validation for the same release branch.

The SHA-pinned helper passes the immutable commit through `ref` and the canonical release branch through `target_context_ref`. The workflow previously used only `ref` for its concurrency identity and release cancellation predicate, so it lost normal `release/*` replacement behavior.

Observed on the `2026.7.2` release:

- full validation run `29320669525` already had three failed parent lanes but remained active while its plugin prerelease Docker child finished
- replacement run `29321412123` remained pending with zero jobs instead of superseding it

## Why This Change Was Made

Full Release Validation now uses `target_context_ref` as the concurrency identity when present and recognizes a `release/*` target context for `cancel-in-progress`.

Exact-SHA validation remains immutable, while repeated validation for the same canonical release branch and rerun group regains the workflow's intended replacement behavior. Unrelated release branches, SHAs without release context, and different rerun groups remain isolated.

## User Impact

Release operators can restart validation for an exact frozen SHA without waiting for a stale validation's remaining child jobs to drain. This reduces release stalls and avoids duplicate queued umbrella runs.

## Evidence
